name: Metatarsal stress fracture
populations: female and male athletes with low energy availability
athletes with a sudden rise in training load
summary: A repetitive-load bone injury of the metatarsal neck or shaft, most often the second or third. Most heal with load reduction and graded loading, but training load and energy availability must be addressed.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Low-risk sites usually heal with load reduction and graded return; mean return to sport rose from 41.7 days (MRI grade 1) to 98.5 days (grade 4) across all bone stress injury sites

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: More than 90% of athletes return. A return-to-run program can start once the athlete is pain-free in daily activities for 5 consecutive days

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Focal bony tenderness over the second or third metatarsal neck or shaft, with pain on hopping and push-off

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs have low sensitivity early; MRI is highly sensitive and specific, and its grade predicts time to return

keyFacts.label: Risk factors
keyFacts.value: Training-load errors, low energy availability, prior bone stress injury, a higher arch, and long metatarsals or abnormal foot motion

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Stress fractures make up 0.7–20% of sports medicine clinic injuries; the tibia, metatarsals and fibula are the most frequent sites

overview:
A bone stress injury (BSI) is the failure of bone to withstand repetitive load. It lies on a continuum from stress reaction through stress fracture to complete fracture, and it tends to recur [r1]. The metatarsals are among the most frequently affected sites [r2]. Long-distance running and recruit training most often produce second and third metatarsal injuries, and soccer is associated with fifth metatarsal fractures [r3]. Low-risk BSIs of the tibial and metatarsal diaphyses account for more than half of BSIs in runners [r4].

Most metatarsal stress fractures at low-risk sites heal with a period of modified loading and a progressive return to running, but the high recurrence rate means that the causes must be found and addressed: training load, bone-loading mechanics, footwear and, in many athletes, energy availability [r1,r5]. The proximal fifth metatarsal is a high-risk site that behaves differently, with slower healing and a higher risk of delayed union, and it is covered on its own page [r6]. Physiotherapists lead the load management, strengthening and return-to-running program, and screen for the broader causes.

epidemiology.text: Stress fractures account for 0.7–20% of sports medicine clinic injuries, and track-and-field athletes have the highest incidence. The tibia, metatarsals and fibula are the most frequently reported sites. Among track athletes the navicular, tibia and metatarsal are common; in dancers the metatarsals are common, and in military recruits the calcaneus and metatarsals are commonly affected, owing to a sudden increase in running and marching without adequate preparation [r2]. Other reviews give a range of 1–20% of athletic injuries, with about 80% in the lower extremity [r7]. In a systematic review of 32 studies, long-distance running and recruit training often led to second or third metatarsal fractures, while soccer was associated with fifth metatarsal fractures [r3]. Most incidence data are reported for all bone stress injuries together. In a collegiate cohort of 239 female athletes, 25 (10.5%) had a BSI, and cross-country runners contributed 64% of them [r8]. In 156 male collegiate distance runners, 27% had at least one BSI over an average 1.9 years [r9].

intrinsic: Higher foot arch, abnormal inversion or eversion of the foot, and longer metatarsal length or larger metatarsal angles; there is no standardised measurement, so the evidence is inconsistent [r3]

Low energy availability and related risk factors (the female athlete triad, REDs): in female collegiate athletes, moderate-risk and high-risk triad scores carried 2.6 and 3.8 times the risk of a BSI [r8,r5]
Prior bone stress injury: each 1-point rise in the prior BSI score was linked to a 57% higher risk of a later BSI in male distance runners [r9]
Oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea and a prior stress fracture or reaction were independent predictors of BSI in female collegiate athletes [r8]
Diminished first MTP joint function, neuropathy, metabolic disorders and hindfoot malalignment [r10]
Weak calf and foot intrinsic muscles, which reduce the muscles' share of the load (clinical reasoning; strengthening is advised for metatarsal BSIs) [r1]
extrinsic: High exercise intensity, non-adaptive training and inadequate equipment [r3]
A sudden increase in running or marching without preparation, as in new recruits [r2]
Distance running, dance, soccer and military training, depending on the site [r3,r2]
Hard surfaces and worn or unsuitable footwear (modifiable; clinical observation, not established for the metatarsals in the sources cited)

mechanism.summary: A metatarsal stress fracture develops from repetitive loading of the forefoot at push-off, without a single injury moment. The metatarsals act as levers and are bent by ground-reaction and muscle forces thousands of times per run. A BSI results from disruption of the balance between microdamage formation and its removal: it depends on the load applied to bone and on bone's ability to resist load [r1]. When training load rises faster than the bone and its muscles can adapt, microdamage accumulates, a stress reaction develops, and a cortical fracture line can follow. The second and third metatarsals are the most common sites in runners and recruits [r3].
sequence: Training volume or intensity rises quickly (a new training block, track work or recruit marching) without enough time for adaptation [r2].
At each push-off the forefoot is loaded: the ground-reaction force is highest under the metatarsal heads, and the metatarsals bend as the toes extend (mechanical model).
Repeated cycles cause microdamage in the cortex at the metatarsal neck or shaft, most often of the second or third metatarsal [r3].
Bone remodelling removes the damaged bone, but when removal outpaces new bone formation the bone is transiently weaker (mechanistic model).
A stress reaction develops: bone marrow oedema and periosteal reaction appear on MRI and pain starts with loading [r2].
If the athlete keeps loading the foot, a cortical fracture line forms (stress fracture), and a complete fracture can follow [r1].
The athlete has forefoot pain that is first present after sport, then during sport, and finally in daily life and at night.

variants.name: Second or third metatarsal neck or shaft (runners, recruits)
variants.description: The classic low-risk site. It is most often reported in long-distance runners and recruit training [r3].

variants.name: Fifth metatarsal stress fracture
variants.description: Associated with soccer, and at the proximal fifth metatarsal it is a high-risk site with a higher rate of delayed union. Pooled union was 87% after surgery and 56% non-surgically in a systematic review of proximal fifth metatarsal stress fractures [r3,r11].

variants.name: Insufficiency-type fractures
variants.description: Occur at normal loads in bone of low strength, such as with metabolic bone disease, neuropathy or inflammatory disease [r10].

variants.name: Fractures related to foot deformity or altered mechanics
variants.description: A high arch, hindfoot malalignment or reduced first MTP function increase the load on the lesser metatarsals [r10,r3].

anatomy.text: The five metatarsals connect the tarsus and the toes. The second and third metatarsals lie in the central rigid column of the foot, anchored proximally at the tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) joint, and carry high load at push-off. The metatarsal diaphyses are cortical-rich bone: in a meta-analysis, cortical-rich sites such as the tibia and metatarsal healed faster than trabecular-rich sites such as the pelvis, femoral neck and calcaneus [r12]. High-risk stress fracture sites, such as the proximal fifth metatarsal, share high tensile load and low blood flow [r6]. Calf and intrinsic foot muscles absorb and share loading, and strengthening the foot intrinsics is suggested for metatarsal BSIs [r1].

structures.name: Second and third metatarsal neck and shaft
structures.role: The commonest sites of stress fracture in runners and recruits; cortical-rich bone with a good blood supply [r3,r12]

structures.name: Metatarsal cortex and periosteum
structures.role: Resist bending and respond to load by remodelling; periosteal reaction is an early imaging sign [r2]

structures.name: Tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) joint
structures.role: Proximal anchor of the second metatarsal; stiffness here shifts bending load to the metatarsal shaft and neck (mechanical reasoning)

structures.name: Intrinsic foot muscles and toe flexors
structures.role: Share load across the metatarsals and support the arch; strengthening them is advised for metatarsal BSIs [r1]

structures.name: Calf muscles and Achilles tendon
structures.role: Generate push-off force and set the load passing through the forefoot

structures.name: Proximal fifth metatarsal (contrast)
structures.role: High-risk site with high tensile load and low blood flow; see the fifth metatarsal fracture page [r6]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Bone stress injury is a fatigue failure of bone along a continuum. A stress reaction (bone marrow oedema and periosteal reaction without a visible fracture line) can progress to a stress fracture and, with continued loading, to a complete fracture [r1]. Damage accumulates when microdamage is created faster than remodelling can remove it [r1]; the bone is thought to be transiently weaker while it is remodelled (mechanistic model). Kaeding and Miller graded stress fractures from grade I (asymptomatic stress reaction on imaging) to grade V (nonunion) [r13].

Healing potential varies by location. Most low-risk BSIs heal readily with a period of modified loading [r1]. High-risk sites share high tensile load and low blood flow, have a greater risk of fracture progression, delayed healing and nonunion, and need a more aggressive approach [r6]. In a meta-analysis of 76 studies, the anatomical site influenced return-to-sport timelines and complication rates; the complication rate was highest for BSIs of the femoral neck, tarsal navicular, anterior tibial shaft and fifth metatarsal [r14]. Plain radiographs often appear normal early, while MRI is highly sensitive and specific for marrow oedema, periosteal reaction and subtle fracture lines [r2].

structures.name: Metatarsal cortex (neck or shaft)
structures.effect: Microdamage, then a stress reaction and, if loading continues, a cortical fracture line [r1]

structures.name: Periosteum and marrow
structures.effect: Periosteal reaction and bone marrow oedema on MRI mark the stress reaction [r2]

structures.name: Adjacent soft tissue
structures.effect: Dorsal forefoot swelling and tenderness over the involved metatarsal in many patients

structures.name: Callus and remodelled bone
structures.effect: Radiographic callus or sclerosis appears weeks after symptoms start, and shows that healing is under way

muscles.name: Foot intrinsics and toe flexors
muscles.effect: Share load with bone. Weakness or fatigue is thought to shift more load to the metatarsals, and strengthening is advised for metatarsal BSIs [r1].

muscles.name: Calf (gastrocnemius–soleus)
muscles.effect: Sets the push-off force through the forefoot. Calf strengthening is advised for tibial BSIs and is part of the kinetic chain here [r1].

muscles.name: Hip and trunk muscles
muscles.effect: Influence running mechanics and impact forces; deconditioning during offloading should be avoided with cross-training [r4].

cellular.description: Repeated bending of the metatarsal produces microdamage in the cortex [r1].
In the mechanistic model, osteoclasts remove damaged bone faster than osteoblasts replace it, leaving the bone transiently weaker.
Marrow oedema and periosteal reaction appear, and pain starts with loading [r2].
A cortical fracture line forms and can progress to a complete fracture if load continues [r1].
With modified loading, osteoblasts lay down new bone and the cortex remodels; return to sport took a mean of 41.7 to 98.5 days (MRI grades 1–4) across sites [r12].

systems.effect: Low energy availability (LEA) is the core of REDs, and it is linked to impaired bone health in female and male athletes [r5]. The Female Athlete Triad risk score predicted BSI in female and male runners [r8,r9]. Critics note that most REDs evidence is associational, and many factors can produce the same symptoms, so assess the whole athlete [r15].
Arch height, foot motion, metatarsal morphology, footwear and running mechanics influence bone load. The evidence is inconsistent and unstandardised [r3].
Pain is mechanical and load-related, and it can progress to rest and night pain as the lesion advances. Persistent rest pain should prompt review.
Dietary intake, vitamin D and calcium contribute to bone health. In one trial reviewed, calcium supplementation did not significantly reduce tibial stress fractures [r16].
Athletes may under-report symptoms or hide disordered eating. Mental health interacts with REDs [r5]. Sensitive screening is needed.

grading.system: Kaeding and Miller stress fracture grading (I–V), plus MRI-based BSI grades 1–4 for prognosis

grades.description: Asymptomatic stress reaction on imaging (no pain, no fracture line) [r13].
Pain with no fracture line on imaging [r13].
grades.prognosis: Good prognosis at low-risk sites with modified loading [r1]
Heals with modified loading at low-risk sites; slower than reaction-only injuries
Needs orthopaedic review; surgical fixation may be required
Needs orthopaedic review; surgical treatment is usually needed

grades.description: A separate MRI grading scheme: higher grades predict a longer return to sport. Mean time to return to sport was 41.7 days for grade 1, 70.1 for grade 2, 84.3 for grade 3 and 98.5 for grade 4 [r12].
grades.prognosis: Longer time to return with higher grade; individual adaptation of rehabilitation is needed [r12]

timeframes.summary: Healing time depends on severity and site. Across all bone stress injury sites, mean return to sport rose from 41.7 days (MRI grade 1) to 98.5 days (grade 4), and metatarsals are cortical-rich sites that healed faster than trabecular-rich sites [r12]. The phases below are typical and overlap.

healing.description: Initial load reduction, with partial or non-weight-bearing if needed, until daily activities are pain-free [r4]
Walking volume, strengthening and cross-training, with pain-guided loading [r4]
Return-to-run program, volume before speed; return took 41.7–98.5 days depending on MRI grade [r4,r12]
Bone remodels along lines of load; keep strength, load management and an energy availability plan to reduce recurrence [r1]

milestones.label: Pain-free daily activities for 5 consecutive days
milestones.note: The criterion used to start a return-to-run program [r4]; time varies with severity

milestones.label: Mean return to sport, MRI grade 1
Mean return to sport, MRI grade 2
Mean return to sport, MRI grade 3
Mean return to sport, MRI grade 4

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based and symptom-driven. More than 90% of athletes return to sport after BSIs [r14]. For a typical low-risk metatarsal injury, expect about 6–14 weeks, depending on severity and MRI grade [r12]. Start a return-to-run program once pain-free in daily activities for 5 consecutive days, and progress volume before speed [r4].

symptoms: Gradual onset of forefoot pain over days to weeks, often after a rise in running volume, track work or marching
Pain first after activity, then during activity, with push-off and hopping provoking it
Pain that eases with rest, then in advanced injury, pain with walking and at night
Localised pain in the middle of the forefoot over a second or third metatarsal
Dorsal forefoot swelling in some, and a limp as symptoms increase
signs: Focal bony tenderness over the neck or shaft of one metatarsal, usually the second or third
Mild dorsal swelling or warmth over the involved metatarsal
Pain on single-leg hop or forefoot loading (toe-raise)
Normal motion at the ankle and MTP joints, with no joint effusion

subjective: Pain behaviour: onset, site, relation to running, and whether it now hurts in daily life or at night
Training load: recent increases in volume, intensity, track work, hills, surface and footwear changes [r2,r3]
Previous bone stress injuries or fractures [r9,r8]
Energy availability and eating: restrictive eating, weight loss, fatigue, mood; menstrual history (oligomenorrhoea, amenorrhoea), and in males, low libido or low testosterone symptoms [r5,r8]
Diet and bone health: vitamin D, calcium, family history, medications and smoking
Sport, level, season timing and goals; any pressure from coaches or teammates
Neurological or metabolic disease affecting the foot (neuropathy, diabetes) [r10]
observation: Foot posture: high arch, hindfoot alignment, forefoot position and abnormal inversion or eversion [r3]
Gait and running pattern: stride rate, foot strike and push-off
Dorsal swelling, bruising or redness over the metatarsals
palpation: Neck and shaft of each metatarsal along the dorsum, comparing with the other foot (focal bony tenderness over one metatarsal)
Compare with the MTP joints and plantar plates, the interdigital spaces (Morton's neuroma) and the Lisfranc joint
Proximal fifth metatarsal and navicular tenderness (high-risk sites) [r6]
rangeOfMotion: Ankle dorsiflexion and first MTP extension; diminished first MTP function is associated with metatarsal stress fractures [r10]
Subtalar and midfoot mobility, to look for stiffness or abnormal inversion or eversion [r3]
strength: Single-leg heel raise: repetitions and symmetry, only when pain allows
Toe flexor and intrinsic foot strength (short-foot test) [r1]
neuro: Sensation over the forefoot and toes; screen for neuropathy as an insufficiency risk factor [r10]
Tinel's and web-space compression if neural pain is suspected
functional: Single-leg hop in place (pain is a positive provocation); avoid repeated hopping if a high-risk site or a displaced fracture is suspected
Walking and running gait with pain rating
Single-leg stance and squat for lower-limb control

specialTests.name: Bony palpation of the metatarsal neck and shaft
specialTests.purpose: Localise the stress injury to a single metatarsal
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the dorsal and lateral aspect of each metatarsal neck and shaft in turn, comparing with the other foot.
specialTests.positive: Focal bony tenderness reproducing the familiar pain. No accuracy figures were identified in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Single-leg hop test
specialTests.procedure: Ask the patient to hop in place on the affected leg a few times, only if there is no suspicion of a high-risk or displaced fracture.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of forefoot pain over the metatarsal. No accuracy figures were identified, and it should not be repeated to the point of aggravation.

specialTests.name: Percussion or tuning-fork test over the metatarsal
specialTests.purpose: Supportive test for a bone stress injury
specialTests.procedure: Tap along the metatarsal shaft or apply a vibrating tuning fork and note any focal pain.
specialTests.positive: Focal pain over the bone. No accuracy data were identified in the sources reviewed; use only with imaging if the diagnosis is uncertain.

specialTests.name: Metatarsal head and interdigital compression
specialTests.purpose: Distinguish stress fracture from forefoot soft-tissue pain (MTP, plantar plate, Morton's neuroma)
specialTests.procedure: Squeeze the forefoot from side to side and palpate the web spaces and the MTP joints.
specialTests.positive: Pain over the web space or MTP joint suggests a neuroma or plantar plate problem rather than a metatarsal shaft fracture. No accuracy figures were identified.

clinicalRules.name: No validated clinical prediction rule
clinicalRules.description: Diagnosis is clinical (history of load increase and focal bony tenderness) and is confirmed by imaging when uncertain. Plain radiography is useful when positive but has low sensitivity early [r2].

clinicalRules.name: REDs Clinical Assessment Tool (Version 2) and Female Athlete Triad Cumulative Risk Assessment
clinicalRules.description: Risk-stratification tools for low energy availability and bone health. The IOC 2023 consensus introduced the REDs Clinical Assessment Tool version 2, with severity and risk stratification and training recommendations [r5]. A modified triad cumulative risk score predicted BSI in female and male runners [r8,r9].

outcomeMeasures.name: Numeric pain rating (0–10) during daily activities, walking, hopping and running
outcomeMeasures.use: Symptom-driven loading: the optimal load does not produce symptoms during, after or the day after loading [r4]

outcomeMeasures.name: Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) with sport subscale, or Foot Function Index
Single-leg heel raise repetitions and hop tolerance
outcomeMeasures.use: Capacity measures to guide loading and return to running

outcomeMeasures.name: Weekly running volume log and next-morning pain
outcomeMeasures.use: Track the return-to-run program and detect flares early [r4]

outcomeMeasures.name: MRI grade (1–4)
outcomeMeasures.use: Prognostic information on time to return to sport, which rises from 41.7 to 98.5 days across grades 1–4 [r12]

imaging.indication: Initial imaging when a bone stress injury is suspected, mainly to exclude other pathology and to monitor healing
imaging.findings: Often normal early because of low sensitivity; later shows periosteal reaction, callus or a fracture line [r2]

imaging.indication: The most sensitive and specific test; use when radiographs are normal, the site is high-risk, or grading and prognosis are needed
imaging.findings: Bone marrow oedema, periosteal reaction and subtle fracture lines; the MRI grade predicts time to return to sport [r2,r12]

imaging.indication: Rarely used now; highly sensitive but not specific, and cannot show a fracture line directly
To define a fracture line, displacement or union in a complex or high-risk case, or when MRI is not possible
imaging.findings: Cortical fracture line, sclerosis, and union or nonunion

differentials.name: Morton's neuroma
differentials.distinguishing: Burning or numbness into adjacent toes, pain in the web space, a positive Mulder's click or web-space compression; no focal bony tenderness.

differentials.name: Lisfranc (tarsometatarsal) injury
differentials.distinguishing: Midfoot pain at the base of the second metatarsal after a twist or axial load, plantar bruising, and pain on twisting the midfoot; imaging shows widening.

differentials.name: Fifth metatarsal fracture (Jones or avulsion)
differentials.distinguishing: Lateral foot pain at the base or proximal shaft of the fifth metatarsal. It is a high-risk site with a higher risk of delayed union [r6].

differentials.name: Navicular stress fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Vague dorsal midfoot or arch pain with tenderness at the navicular 'N-spot'; high-risk site where imaging is essential [r6].

differentials.name: Sesamoid injury
differentials.distinguishing: Pain under the first metatarsal head, worse on push-off and with toe extension.

differentials.name: Freiberg's infraction or MTP synovitis and plantar plate injury
differentials.distinguishing: Pain at the second metatarsal head or MTP joint, swelling and restricted joint motion; Freiberg's occurs in adolescents. Imaging distinguishes.

differentials.name: Extensor tendinopathy or dorsal foot soft-tissue overload
differentials.distinguishing: Pain along the extensor tendons that is worse with resisted toe extension or tight laces, with no focal bony tenderness.

differentials.name: Infection, tumour or Charcot arthropathy
differentials.distinguishing: Constant or night pain, swelling and warmth, fever or systemic features, or diabetes and neuropathy; arrange urgent medical review.

redFlags: Constant rest pain, night pain, fever, unexplained weight loss or a history of cancer: suspect infection, tumour or a more advanced fracture. Arrange urgent imaging and medical review.
Pain at a high-risk site (proximal fifth metatarsal, navicular, base of the second metatarsal) or a displaced or complete fracture: do not load; refer for orthopaedic review [r6].

Multiple or recurrent stress fractures, amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea, disordered eating, low BMI or low bone density: screen for REDs and refer for medical, nutritional and mental health assessment [r5,r8].
No progress after about 12 weeks of well-delivered load management, or pain returning with graded loading: suspect delayed union or nonunion and refer for imaging (clinical convention).
Diabetes, neuropathy or poor circulation with forefoot pain, swelling or warmth: urgent review for Charcot change, infection or ischaemia.
Sudden severe pain with a pop and inability to bear weight during sport: suspect a complete or displaced fracture and arrange radiographs.

management.principles: Treat a low-risk metatarsal stress fracture as a bone load–capacity problem. Reduce load until daily activities are pain-free, then build load with symptom-driven loading: the optimal load does not produce symptoms during, after or the day after loading [r4]. Find and treat the causes: training-load errors, running mechanics and footwear, foot and calf strength, and energy availability and bone health [r1,r5]. The evidence is mostly expert-based and observational; the optimal-loading approach is clinically successful but still needs scientific validation [r4]. High-risk sites such as the proximal fifth metatarsal and the navicular need a more aggressive approach, often non-weight-bearing immobilisation or surgery [r6,r14].

medical.name: Medical, nutritional and bone-health assessment (REDs screen)
medical.description: For athletes with recurrent or multiple BSIs or risk features (menstrual dysfunction, low BMI, restrictive eating): use the REDs Clinical Assessment Tool, and arrange a doctor, dietitian and, when needed, psychologist. The IOC consensus gives prevention and treatment principles; critics note most evidence is associational [r5,r15].

medical.name: Short-term analgesia
medical.description: Simple analgesics or NSAIDs, in the short term only (less than 7 days), and only for resting pain and night pain [r4].

medical.name: Walking boot, partial or non-weight-bearing
medical.description: An initial period of load reduction, via partial or non-weight-bearing, is typically needed to relieve symptoms [r4]. Evidence for pneumatic bracing comes from tibial stress fractures, where it shortened time to return to full activity [r16].

medical.name: Healing adjuncts (low-intensity pulsed ultrasound, recombinant parathyroid hormone)
medical.description: These 'healing supplements' may be attempted to influence tissue healing, but they are not established for metatarsal BSIs [r4].

medical.name: Surgical fixation (displaced fracture, nonunion, or high-risk site)
medical.description: For grade IV–V stress fractures and high-risk sites. Surgery is recommended for fifth metatarsal stress fractures in athletes [r10]. In a systematic review of proximal fifth metatarsal stress fractures, pooled union was 87% after surgery and 56% non-surgically, with low study quality [r11]. It is not needed for typical second or third metatarsal fractures.

physio.name: Education and symptom-driven load management
physio.description: Explain the continuum from stress reaction to fracture and why symptoms are the guide. Keep load at a level that causes no symptoms during, after or the day following loading [r4].

physio.name: Cross-training and strength to keep fitness
physio.description: Cycling, pool running, swimming and upper-body or core work, while addressing musculoskeletal fitness at the same time [r4].

physio.name: Graded return-to-run program
physio.description: Start once the athlete is pain-free in daily activities for 5 consecutive days. Progress is symptom-guided and increases running volume before speed [r4].

physio.name: Foot intrinsic and calf strengthening
physio.description: Strengthening the foot intrinsics for metatarsal BSIs and the calf to share load and reduce bone strain [r1].

physio.name: Gait retraining and impact reduction
physio.description: Running 'softer' or with a higher stride rate to reduce impact forces, and addressing malalignment and abnormal movement patterns; it may also reduce subsequent BSI risk [r1,r4].

physio.name: Jump training after return
physio.description: Optimal loading after return may include jump training to reduce later BSI risk [r4].

physio.name: Shock-absorbing insoles or orthoses
physio.description: The original Cochrane review pooled four trials in athletes and military personnel and found that shock-absorbing insoles reduced stress fractures and stress reactions (Peto OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.30–0.76) [r17]. A later appraisal of the Cochrane update found that none of the four trials was individually significant, only limited evidence of benefit, and that the best design is unknown [r16]. The trials are in military recruits and are mostly tibial.

physio.name: Continuing full training through pain
physio.description: Bone stress injuries lie on a continuum and can progress from reaction to fracture if loading continues [r1].

physio.name: Prolonged complete unloading beyond symptom relief
physio.description: Unloading is needed only until symptoms ease [r4]; longer rest causes deconditioning and does not build the bone's capacity.

education: A stress fracture is a fatigue injury: the bone has been loaded faster than it could adapt. Most heal well with a planned period of modified load.
Pain is your guide. Load should not cause pain during, after or the next day.
Keep fit while you heal: cycling, pool work and upper-body and core training do not load the foot.
Running starts again once daily life has been pain-free for five days, with volume first and speed later.
Eating enough for your training matters for bone health. Tell us about any dieting, missed periods or tiredness so we can help.
Stress fractures can come back. Fixing the cause (training load, nutrition, footwear and strength) reduces the risk [r1].

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and symptom-driven. The optimal load does not produce symptoms during, after or the day following loading, and it is increased only when this holds [r4]. The stages are: offload and settle, restore capacity, return to running, and return to sport with prevention. Stage timeframes are typical and depend on severity (return to sport took a mean of 41.7 to 98.5 days across MRI grades) [r12]. Dosages are typical clinical ranges drawn from clinical practice and from the principles in the optimal-load paper, not prescriptions from a single trial [r4]. Address training load, footwear, strength and energy availability throughout [r1,r5].

stages.name: Offload & settle
goals: Relieve pain with initial load reduction (partial or non-weight-bearing if needed)
Educate on cause, symptom-driven loading and energy availability
precautions: Avoid hopping and running until pain-free in daily life
Use a boot or crutches if walking is painful [r4]
Screen red flags (high-risk site, REDs, night pain) before loading

exercises.name: Cycling or pool running (non-impact cardiovascular)
exercises.dosage: 30–45 min, 4–5 times a week, below the pain threshold
exercises.cues: Maintain aerobic fitness without forefoot impact

exercises.name: Glute bridge
exercises.cues: Drive through the heels and keep the ribs down

exercises.name: Side-lying clamshell
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis still and the foot relaxed

exercises.name: Dead bug (core)
exercises.cues: Press the low back into the mat

exercises.name: Seated calf raise (light, pain-free)
exercises.cues: Gentle effort, no pain at the metatarsal

exercises.name: Short-foot (intrinsic) activation
exercises.cues: Draw the ball of the foot toward the heel without curling the toes

progressionCriteria: Pain-free daily activities for 5 consecutive days [r4]
No focal bony tenderness over the metatarsal
Walks 20–30 min with pain at or below 2/10

stages.name: Restore capacity
goals: Return to normal walking volume without a limp
Build calf and foot intrinsic strength
precautions: Increase load only if the previous session settled by the next day [r4]
Keep pain at or below about 2/10 and settled by the next morning (clinical convention)

exercises.name: Double-leg calf raise
exercises.dosage: 3 × 12–15, 3 s up and 3 s down, daily
exercises.cues: Weight over the whole forefoot, even through the big toe

exercises.name: Single-leg calf raise
exercises.cues: Full range with a pause at the top

exercises.name: Bodyweight squat
exercises.cues: Whole foot on the floor and the knee over the second toe

exercises.name: Single-leg balance (short foot)
exercises.cues: Keep the arch lifted and the big toe down

exercises.name: Walking program
exercises.dosage: Build to 45–60 min, 4–5 times a week on level ground
exercises.cues: Even push-off through the whole forefoot

progressionCriteria: Walks 45–60 min with no pain during or the next day
Single-leg calf raise × 15 with no forefoot pain (clinical convention)
No tenderness at the fracture site and a normal gait

stages.name: Return to running
goals: Restart running in a graded way
Build impact tolerance with hopping and jumping
precautions: Start only after pain-free daily activities for 5 consecutive days [r4]
Progress running volume before speed, and allow rest days between runs
Step back if pain appears during, after or the next day [r4]

exercises.name: Walk–run program on soft, level surfaces
exercises.dosage: 1 min run / 2 min walk for 20 min, every second day, adding running as the next day stays symptom-free (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Short, quick steps and a soft landing

exercises.name: Continuous running with volume progression
exercises.dosage: Build total weekly run time by about 10% as symptoms allow (clinical convention); speed work last
exercises.cues: Check the foot the morning after each run

exercises.name: Single-leg hop in place, then forward
exercises.dosage: 3 × 5–8 each leg, twice a week once running is tolerated
exercises.cues: Soft landing and stick for 2 s

exercises.name: Step-up with heel drive
exercises.cues: Control the pelvis and push through the whole foot

exercises.name: Heavy calf and foot strength maintenance
exercises.cues: Slow tempo and full range

progressionCriteria: Runs 30 min continuously with pain at or below 1–2/10 and no next-morning increase [r4]
No focal tenderness at the fracture site
Stable weekly volume for 2 weeks without a flare

stages.name: Return to sport & prevention
goals: Return to sport-specific running, cutting and jumping
Return to full training and competition
Keep strength, jump training and load monitoring
Resolve the contributing causes (load, footwear, energy availability)
precautions: Increase training load by steps, not spikes
Do not return to competition while pain is present during or the day after sport
Keep monitoring energy availability and bone health [r5]

exercises.name: Planned then reactive change of direction
exercises.dosage: 2 sessions a week, increasing speed and angle
exercises.cues: Land under control, knee over the foot

exercises.name: Jump training (low to moderate height)
exercises.cues: Soft landing with hips and knees bent

exercises.name: Graded team training or race-pace work
exercises.cues: Share the plan with the coach and monitor pain and load

exercises.name: Gait retraining (higher stride rate, softer landing)
exercises.dosage: Short blocks within running sessions, 2–3 times a week
exercises.cues: Quiet steps and a slightly higher cadence

exercises.name: Heavy strength maintenance (calf, foot, hip)
exercises.cues: Keep loads heavy and the tempo controlled

progressionCriteria: Full training for at least 2 weeks with no pain during or the next day [r4]
Single-leg calf raise × 20 and hop tests pain-free and symmetrical (clinical convention)
Contributing causes addressed: training plan, footwear and nutrition plan
Athlete, coach and clinician agree on the return

criteria: No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria were identified for metatarsal stress fractures; the criteria below reflect the symptom-driven approach and clinical convention [r4]
Pain-free daily activities for at least 5 consecutive days before starting running [r4]
No focal bony tenderness, and a pain-free single-leg hop and single-leg calf raise × 20 (clinical convention)
Graded running progressed from volume to speed with no pain during, after or the next day [r4]
Completion of full, unrestricted training for at least 2 weeks without a flare
Cause addressed: load plan, footwear, strength, and a medical and nutritional review where risk features were present [r5]
tests: Palpation of the metatarsal and pain rating during hopping
Single-leg heel raise repetitions and symmetry
Single-leg hop tests with pain rating
Weekly running volume log and next-morning pain
REDs Clinical Assessment Tool or triad risk screen [r5,r8]
Repeat imaging only if symptoms persist or the site is high-risk

prognosis: The prognosis for low-risk metatarsal stress fractures is good: most heal with modified loading and a progressive return to running [r1]. In a meta-analysis of 76 studies, more than 90% of athletes returned to sport, although anatomical site influenced timelines and complications [r14]. Mean return to sport across all sites ranged from 41.7 days for MRI grade 1 to 98.5 days for grade 4, and cortical-rich sites such as the metatarsals healed faster than trabecular-rich sites [r12]. BSIs tend to recur: runners with a prior BSI had a higher risk of another, and the risk rose with the cumulative risk score [r1,r9]. The complication rate was highest for BSIs of the femoral neck, navicular, anterior tibia and fifth metatarsal [r14]. For proximal fifth metatarsal stress fractures, pooled union was 87% after surgery and 56% non-surgically, with a 33% nonunion rate in the non-surgical group; study quality was low [r11].
prevention: Progress training load gradually and avoid sudden jumps in running or marching volume or intensity, with adequate recovery [r2,r3].

Screen athletes for low energy availability and bone health risk (REDs Clinical Assessment Tool, triad risk assessment) and treat the cause with a doctor and dietitian [r5,r8,r9]. The REDs model is debated, and most evidence is associational, so assess the whole athlete [r15].
Maintain calf and foot intrinsic strength all year [r1].
Address malalignment, abnormal movement patterns and impact loading, for example with a higher stride rate and softer landings (expert opinion) [r1].
Use well-fitting, supportive footwear and consider shock-absorbing insoles; evidence is conflicting and no single design is best [r17,r16].
Track prior BSI, because a previous BSI predicts another [r9].
clinicalPearls: Focal bony tenderness over a second or third metatarsal plus a recent rise in load is a stress fracture until proven otherwise. Normal plain radiographs do not exclude it, because their sensitivity is low early; MRI is highly sensitive and specific [r2].

Know the site. Second and third metatarsal neck and shaft are low-risk and managed with load modification. The proximal fifth metatarsal and the navicular are high-risk and need a more aggressive approach [r6,r14].
Let symptoms set the load: the right load does not hurt during, after or the day after, and a return-to-run program starts once daily life is pain-free for 5 days [r4].

Ask about eating, menstrual function and energy. Moderate and high triad risk scores carried 2.6 and 3.8 times the risk of a BSI in female collegiate athletes, and a modified score also predicted BSI in male runners [r8,r9].
A previous BSI is a strong predictor of the next one, so fix the cause as well as the bone [r9,r1].
Use MRI grade to set expectations: mean return to sport rose from 41.7 days (grade 1) to 98.5 days (grade 4) across sites [r12].

animation.title: How a metatarsal stress fracture develops

captions.text: A runner steps up training: more miles and more track work, with little time to adapt.
At each push-off the weight is carried on the forefoot and the metatarsals bend.
That load is repeated thousands of times in every run.
Bone constantly repairs microdamage, but only as fast as its biology allows.
When load rises faster than repair, microdamage accumulates in a metatarsal.
There is no single injury: forefoot pain builds over days to weeks.
Zooming into the right foot, viewed from above (dorsal view).

actions.text: Stress reaction at the neck: damage outpaces repair

captions.text: The second and third metatarsals are the most common stress fracture sites in runners and recruits.
At push-off the ground pushes up through the metatarsal heads and bends the bones.
With repeated loading, the cortex of the metatarsal neck develops microdamage.
Pain is focal over the bone and is provoked by push-off and hopping.
A stress reaction develops: bone marrow oedema and periosteal reaction show on MRI.
If loading continues, a cortical fracture line forms: a stress fracture.
Most heal with load reduction and graded loading, unlike high-risk sites such as the proximal fifth metatarsal.
Healthy bone: an ordered network of osteocytes and mineralised collagen in balance.
Loading: each step bends the bone slightly and stimulates adaptation.
Microdamage: repeated cycles create tiny cracks faster than normal.
Remodelling removes the damaged bone faster than new bone is laid down, so the bone is briefly weaker.
Stress reaction: marrow oedema and periosteal reaction appear, and it hurts to load.
Stress fracture: a crack runs through the cortex if loading continues.
Healing: with modified load, osteoblasts rebuild the bone and the cortex remodels.
